Migrating

a document is different: it rewrites the document so that it targets a later draft, and means exactly what it meant. This chapter defines the migration from every earlier draft to this one, once, as a function of the document and the target, so that every migrator writes the same bytes and nothing is lost on the way.
Migrations and migrators
A
migrator

target

migration
of the document to M. A migration is made of

moved

A migrator MUST write the migration of a document to a draft — the document this chapter defines — exactly as step 2 of
writes a value: its members sorted, two spaces of indentation, a final line feed.
A migration omits no default: step 1 of

is the canonical form's, and a migration changes only what its steps change. So the migration of a document in canonical form — as every document a tool stores is — is in canonical form itself, and the migration of any other document has the canonical form of the migration of its canonical form whenever the document is valid.
The migration of a document to the draft it declares MUST be the document itself.

The migration of a document from a draft N to a later draft M MUST be the result of applying every step from N to M in order: from 0.1 to 0.3, the step from 0.2 to 0.3 applied to the result of the step from 0.1 to 0.2.
A migration MUST NOT change anything in a document but what its steps change: the version declaration, the members they move, and the record of what they moved (
A migration is therefore a deterministic function of the document and the target alone. It does not depend on the extensions a migrator implements, on the known extensions it is configured with (
), on the files of a package, on a clock or on a network; and every other member of the document, the content of extension data and of
included, comes through unchanged, as
and
require of every writer. Its content hash (
) is its own: a migrated document declares another draft, so its canonical form and its hash differ from the original's (except when the target is the draft it declares).
A migrator of this draft migrates documents of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 to any of those drafts that is not earlier than the one they declare.

What a migration preserves

A step changes nothing a reader of the later draft derives anything from. The members it moves are ones a reader of that draft does not read in the document the step is given — opaque extension data, an extension element's own member (
) — and does not read in
either; and with the version declared, everything else is read as it was. So a reader of the target reads the migration of a document exactly as it reads the document.

A reader of the target draft that implements no extension and is configured with no known extensions MUST report for the migration of a document the validity and the diagnostics it reports for the document, and derive from it exactly the values it derives from the document.

Previous versions and later majors
Floorspec follows Semantic Versioning (

). Each major version of the specification ships a normative migration from the major before it — a chapter like this one, with its conformance tests — and a reference migrator; and a reader of a major reads documents of the major before it, either as

reads them or by migrating them on load. While the major version is 0 every draft is a major in this sense: the version before a draft is the draft before it, so the migrations of this chapter are from 0.1 and 0.2, and a reader of this draft reads documents of 0.2, and of 0.1 too (
). Floorspec 1.0 will read documents of the last 0.x draft and ship the migration from it.
The reference migrators of this draft are the conformance oracle's (
in the standard's repository), from which the suite's expected outputs are made, and D3 Floorspec's (
), which passes the suite.
